title: Can hurricanes be moderated or diverted?

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: Every year huge rotating storms packing winds greater than 120 kilometers per hour sweep across tropical seas and onto shorelines. When these storms – called hurricanes in the Atlantic and the eastern Pacific oceans – strike heavily populated areas, they can cause injury and loss of life and lead to billions of dollars of property damage. And nothing, absolutely nothing, stands in their way. But must these fearful forces of nature be forever beyond our control? My research colleagues and I think not. Our team is investigating how we might learn to move hurricanes onto more benign paths or otherwise defuse them.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: To see why hurricanes may be susceptible to human intervention, one must understand their nature and origins. Hurricanes grow as clusters of thunderstorms over the tropical oceans. These waters continuously provide heat and moisture to the atmosphere, producing warm, humid air above the sea surface. When this air rises, the water vapor in it condenses to form clouds and precipitation. Condensation releases heat – that is, the heat from the sun which evaporated the water from the ocean surface at the beginning of the process. This heat that is released makes the air more buoyant, causing it to ascend still higher. Eventually the tropical depression begins to organize and strengthen, creating the 'eye' – the calm central hub around which the hurricane spins. On reaching land, the hurricane's sustaining source of warm water is cut off, and this causes the storm to weaken rapidly.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: Our current studies grew out of an intuition I had 30 years ago when I was a graduate student learning about chaos theory. A chaotic system is one that appears to behave randomly but is, in fact, governed by rules. It is also highly sensitive to initial conditions, so that seemingly insignificant, arbitrary inputs can have profound effects that lead quickly to unpredictable consequences. In the case of hurricanes, small changes in such features as the ocean's temperature, the location of the large-scale wind currents, or even the shape of the rain clouds can strongly influence a hurricane's potential path and power. I was not able to pursue these ideas back then, but in the past decade computer simulation and remote-sensing technologies have advanced enough to renew my interest in large-scale weather control.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: Currently, my colleagues and I are employing detailed computer models of hurricanes to try to identify the kinds of action that might eventually be attempted. In particular, we simulate the behavior of past hurricanes and then test the effects of various interventions by observing changes in the modeled storms. Then we used this target to create artificial meteorological observations and fed these into the weather forecast system. We set the computer to calculate the smallest change to the initial set of the hurricane's key defining properties.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: The most significant modifications proved to be in the starting temperatures and winds. Typical temperature adjustments were only tenths of a degree, but the most notable change was an increase of nearly two degrees Celsius. The calculations revealed wind-speed alterations of four or five kilometers per hour. In a few locations, though, the velocities changed by 30 kilometers per hour because of minor redirections of the winds near the storm's center. Contrary to all our expectations, our first experiment had worked. Although the original and altered versions of Hurricane Iniki looked nearly identical in structure, the changes were large enough to cause the storm to veer off to the west, so that Kauai escaped the most damaging winds and thus, if this had not been a simulation, many fatalities and considerable damage would have been avoided.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: If it is true, as our results suggest, that small changes in the temperature in and around a hurricane can shift its path in a predictable direction or slow its winds, the question becomes, how can such perturbations be achieved? No-one, of course, can alter the temperature throughout something as large as a hurricane instantaneously. It might be possible, however, to heat the air around a hurricane and thus adjust the temperature over time. Undoubtedly, the energy required to do so would be huge, but an array of solar power stations orbiting in space around the Earth could eventually be constructed to supply sufficient energy. These satellites might use giant mirrors to focus sunlight on solar cells and then beam the collected energy down to microwave receivers on the ground. By tuning the microwave linking device to frequencies that are better absorbed by water vapor, different levels of the atmosphere could be heated as desired.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: Another potential method to modify hurricanes would be to directly limit the availability of energy, by coating the ocean surface with a thin film of a biodegradable oil that slows evaporation. Thus, by altering air pressure, changes could be stimulated in the large-scale wind patterns which can have major effects on a hurricane's intensity and track. Further, relatively minor alterations to our normal activities – such as directing aircraft flight plans to precisely position condensation trails and thus increase cloud cover, or varying crop irrigation practices to enhance or decrease evaporation – might generate the appropriate starting alterations.
